mu-c056fed9.stem: Which nerve descends on the anterior surface of scalenus anterior?
mu-c056fed9.explanation: The phrenic nerve (C3–C5) descends beneath the prevertebral fascia on the anterior surface of scalenus anterior, running from lateral to medial, and enters the thorax through the thoracic inlet. The front of the scalene muscle is therefore an important surgical landmark.

mu-271e8cb9.stem: Which structures pass through the gap between scalenus anterior and scalenus medius?
options: Common carotid artery and vagus nerve
Subclavian artery and the roots/trunks of the brachial plexus
Internal jugular vein and thoracic duct
mu-271e8cb9.explanation: The subclavian artery and brachial plexus pass through the scalene gap; the subclavian vein passes in front of scalenus anterior. Hypertrophy or anomalies of the scalenes can cause thoracic outlet syndrome in this gap. The interscalene block is given here.

mu-a90185dc.stem: Which of the following suprahyoid muscle–nerve pairings is WRONG?
options: Digastric, anterior belly – nerve to mylohyoid
mu-a90185dc.explanation: Geniohyoid is supplied by C1 fibres, which travel with the hypoglossal nerve. The two bellies of digastric have different nerves (V3 and VII) because they develop from different pharyngeal arches.

mu-fc270dfa.stem: What supplies most of the infrahyoid muscles?
mu-fc270dfa.explanation: Sternohyoid, sternothyroid and omohyoid are supplied by the ansa cervicalis. Thyrohyoid receives C1 fibres travelling with the hypoglossal nerve. The superior root of the ansa (C1) runs with XII, the inferior root comes from C2–C3.

mu-e6429da9.explanation: Platysma is a thin muscle of facial expression lying in the superficial cervical fascia, supplied by the cervical branch of the facial nerve. It tenses the skin of the neck and pulls the corner of the mouth down.

mu-c93345cd.stem: After a lymph node biopsy from the posterior triangle of the neck, a patient's shoulder droops and he has difficulty raising the arm above 90° and shrugging. Which nerve and muscle are injured?
mu-c93345cd.explanation: The accessory nerve runs superficially in the posterior triangle and is easily injured in biopsies. The upper fibres of trapezius elevate the scapula and, with serratus anterior, rotate it upwards; when paralysed the shoulder droops and abduction above 90° becomes difficult.

mu-0436982a.explanation: The thoracodorsal nerve (C6–C8) arises from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus. Latissimus dorsi extends, adducts and internally rotates the arm; it is powerful in climbing and swimming. It is used as a flap in reconstructive surgery.

mu-82af24b8.explanation: The dorsal scapular nerve arises directly from the C5 root, pierces scalenus medius and supplies levator scapulae and the rhomboids. The rhomboids pull the scapula backwards and upwards towards the spine.

mu-d6c0781b.stem: Which nerves supply the deep (intrinsic) back muscles such as erector spinae?
options: Anterior rami of the spinal nerves
Posterior rami of the spinal nerves
mu-d6c0781b.explanation: The true back muscles (erector spinae, transversospinal and suboccipital muscles) are epaxial in origin and are supplied segmentally by the posterior rami of the spinal nerves. The superficial back muscles (trapezius, latissimus, rhomboids) belong to the limb and receive nerves derived from anterior rami.

mu-33067b41.stem: Which artery runs in the floor of the suboccipital triangle, over the posterior arch of the atlas?
mu-33067b41.explanation: The suboccipital triangle is bounded by rectus capitis posterior major and obliquus capitis superior and inferior. In its floor, in the groove on the posterior arch of the atlas, lie the vertebral artery and the suboccipital nerve (posterior ramus of C1). The greater occipital nerve passes over the triangle.

mu-4dfb1e53.stem: Which structures bound the inferior lumbar triangle (Petit's triangle)?
options: Inguinal ligament, rectus abdominis and inferior epigastric artery
Quadratus lumborum, psoas major and diaphragm
Trapezius, latissimus dorsi and the medial border of the scapula
Erector spinae, 12th rib and internal oblique
Latissimus dorsi, external oblique and the iliac crest
mu-4dfb1e53.explanation: Petit's triangle lies between latissimus dorsi (posteromedially), external oblique (anterolaterally) and the iliac crest (base); its floor is formed by the internal oblique. Rare lumbar hernias can develop here. Trapezius, latissimus and the scapular border bound the triangle of auscultation.

mu-01a8ca30.stem: After mastectomy and axillary dissection, when the patient stretches the arms forwards and pushes against a wall, the medial border of the scapula lifts off the chest wall (winged scapula). Which nerve is injured?
mu-01a8ca30.explanation: The long thoracic nerve (C5–C7) descends on the outer surface of serratus anterior along the medial wall of the axilla and is easily injured in axillary surgery. Serratus anterior presses the scapula against the chest wall and protracts it; when paralysed the scapula wings and the arm cannot be raised above 90°.

mu-31bba149.stem: What is the nerve supply of pectoralis major?
mu-31bba149.explanation: Pectoralis major is supplied by the lateral (C5–C7) and medial (C8–T1) pectoral nerves. It adducts and internally rotates the arm; its clavicular head flexes and its sternocostal head extends.

mu-f9d2c90b.stem: Which muscle divides the axillary artery into three parts?
mu-f9d2c90b.explanation: The axillary artery runs from the outer border of the 1st rib to the lower border of teres major; the part above pectoralis minor is the 1st part, behind it the 2nd and below it the 3rd. Pectoralis minor also divides the levels of the axillary lymph nodes.
